fields.expected:
I'd want to work on evaluation infrastructure for AI systems, either inside an early-stage company building it or as something I start myself. That interest came out of specific work. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes rather than just reporting aggregate accuracy. Generating an answer with an LLM turned out to be the cheap part; deciding whether it should be trusted was the hard part. That has shaped almost everything I've built since. In my job-application agent, I made free-text essays and demographic fields architecturally impossible to autofill, and I built a validation ladder so a capability isn't called working just because it passes a local fixture. In tSearch, missing evidence returns "insufficient evidence" instead of a low score.

The other thing I'd be drawn to is research infrastructure. I've spent the past year studying how research gets funded and selected, talking with researchers, administrators, and people building alternative research organizations. My current hypothesis is that AI is making scientific generation abundant while judgment stays scarce, so I'd want to build systems for methodological validation, provenance, and evidence tracing.

fields.expected:
The hardest one was estimating sleep on ClarityAtlas without requiring a wearable. Most sleep features assume a watch on the wrist overnight, and our pilot users at Hopkins mostly didn't have one. So the only signals available were phone-side: HealthKit and Core Motion data like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns, plus phone-interaction activity. None of those directly say "asleep." They say "the phone stopped moving and nobody touched it," which is also true when someone leaves their phone on a desk for three hours.

I built the estimator in Swift around those inputs and spent most of the effort on the failure cases rather than the happy path: charging periods, late-night phone use before actual sleep, and gaps where no data arrived at all. The part I got wrong initially was treating absence of signal as evidence of sleep, which produced confidently wrong sleep windows. I changed it so low-evidence periods stayed low-confidence instead of being filled in.

We shipped it into a live pilot with 30+ users, which is where most of the edge cases actually surfaced. That experience is why I now assume a system isn't validated until it has been tested against the level of reality it claims to handle.

fields.expected:
During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We walked over to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us get a word in. We pitched ClarityAtlas standing there in the entryway. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute.

I'm proud of it less because of the outcome and more because it was uncomfortable and I did it anyway. I default to thinking the technical work is the real work, and for a long time I assumed a good product would find its own audience. SnapSort taught me otherwise, and ClarityAtlas made it concrete. Recruiting our first pilot users, explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist, and knocking on a locked door mattered as much as anything I wrote in Swift. Nobody was going to schedule that meeting for us. That's a habit I'd rather keep than a line on a resume.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer. The pattern in most of my work is that the technical piece is only half the problem, and the other half is understanding the actual environment the system has to survive in. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps data, and weather information. That only made sense because the real constraint wasn't modeling, it was what care was reachable from a specific village on a specific day. Same with ClarityAtlas: I built the sleep estimation on phone-side HealthKit and Core Motion signals because our Hopkins pilot users didn't have wearables, and I only learned that by putting it in front of 30+ of them. On the Summer Atlantic Capital anomaly-detection system, the thing I keep returning to isn't model performance, it's that an alert system producing too many alerts creates a second problem for analysts. That's why I built the ranking layer and the retrieval-augmented explanation layer. I like being close enough to the user that I can tell when the correct-looking system is still failing them, then going back and changing the design.
